title: At the market
goal: Buy groceries by quantity, point at things, and use verbs that split in the middle.
bekal: using verbs that split in the middle

dialogs.title: Diálogo — En el mercado
dialogs.intro: A traditional market, where prices are per kilo and the queue has rules of its own.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Yo. ¿Qué tal? Quisiera un kilo de tomates.
lines.id: Me. How are you? I'd like a kilo of tomatoes.
lines.literal: I. how-goes? I-would-want a kilo of tomatoes.

lines.speaker: Vendedor:
lines.text: ¿Estos o aquellos? Estos están más maduros.
lines.id: These or those? These are riper.
lines.literal: these or those? these they-are more ripe.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Esos de ahí, por favor. ¿A cuánto están?
lines.id: Those ones, please. How much are they today?
lines.literal: those of there, please. at how-much they-are?

lines.speaker: Vendedor:
lines.text: A dos euros el kilo. Están muy buenos hoy.
lines.id: Two euros a kilo. They're very good today.
lines.literal: at two euros the kilo. they-are very good today.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Vale. Y medio kilo de queso, por favor.
lines.id: OK. And half a kilo of cheese, please.
lines.literal: OK. and half kilo of cheese, please.

lines.speaker: Vendedor:
lines.id: Anything else? I have some very sweet oranges.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: No me gustan mucho las naranjas. ¿Tiene manzanas?

lines.text: Sí, un kilo son tres euros.

lines.id: Then a kilo. How much is everything?

lines.id: Eight euros twenty. Do you have any change?

lines.text: Solo tengo un billete de veinte. Lo siento.

notes: **¿Quién es el último?** is the unwritten queuing rule at Spanish markets: people don't stand in a neat line, they ask who arrived last and remember that face. If someone asks after you arrive, answer *yo*.
**¿A cuánto están?** is for goods whose price changes — vegetables, fruit, fish. *¿Cuánto cuesta?* is for things with a fixed price. Using *cuesta* at the market isn't wrong, just a bit less natural.
**Vale** = "OK", the most-said word in Spain after *hola*. In Latin America the equivalent is *está bien* or *bueno*.

**Quantities use de.** *Un kilo **de** tomates*, *medio kilo **de** queso*, *una botella **de** agua*, *un poco **de** azúcar*. It's like English "of" — except Spanish never drops it: "a little sugar" is still *un poco de azúcar*.
**Están muy buenos** uses *estar*, not *ser* — because it's about how they taste today, not tomatoes in general. Remember the pair *ser bueno* (good) vs *estar bueno* (tasty) from Unit 11.
**No me gustan mucho** = "I'm not so keen on them", much softer than *no me gustan*. Adding *mucho* softens the no, just like "not really" in English.
**Suelto** = loose change or small notes. *Un billete* is a banknote, *una moneda* a coin. You'll hear *¿tiene suelto?* almost every day at the market.
**Lo siento** = "sorry" for something you regret. Different from *perdón / perdone*, used to interrupt or say "excuse me".

grammars.title: Este, ese, aquel — pointing at things
body: Spanish distinguishes **three** distances, not two like English: near the speaker, near the listener, and far from both.
after: All of them can stand alone without a noun: *quiero este* (I want this one), *esos de ahí* (those ones there). The matching place words: *aquí* (here) — *ahí* (there, by you) — *allí* (over there).
There's one more, genderless form: *esto*, *eso*, *aquello*, used for things that don't have a name yet. *¿Qué es esto?* — what's this? You'll never use it in front of a noun.

grammars.title: Verbs that split in the middle
body: A large group of verbs change the vowel in the **stressed syllable**. Since the stress in *nosotros* and *vosotros* falls on the ending, those two rows escape the change — and that's the trademark of the whole group.
after: Other **e→ie** verbs: *empezar* (to begin), *preferir* (to prefer), *entender* (to understand), *pensar* (to think), *cerrar* (to close). **o→ue** verbs: *costar* (to cost), *dormir* (to sleep), *volver* (to come back), *encontrar* (to find), *jugar* (to play, the only u→ue).
Dictionaries don't mark this change, so the safest way is to learn the *yo* form along with the verb from the start: not *poder*, but *poder / puedo*.

blocks.title: No haggling — except in one place
items: In Spanish shops and markets, prices are **not haggled over**. Bargaining at a *mercado* is considered rude. The one place where haggling is normal is *el mercadillo* — the weekly flea market selling secondhand goods and cheap clothes.
Displayed prices already include tax (*IVA*). The number on the label is what you pay — nothing is added at the till, unlike in the United States.
*Las rebajas* is the official sales season, twice a year: January and July. The discounts are real and big, and the first day is incredibly busy.
Commas and periods are the reverse of English: *2,50 €* means two euros fifty, and *1.500 €* means one thousand five hundred. The euro sign also goes after the number.
